title: Testing = Learning
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that teachers should stop calling it retrieval practice and just call it testing. In the classrooms he visits, Do Now retrieval activities are often passive, with half the students waiting to copy down the right answer, whereas the word test makes teachers and students treat the exercise seriously. He then draws on the Bjorks' work, as excerpted in his book The Full English, to set out the testing effect, the superiority of retesting over reteaching, and the value of broad multiple-choice sampling of a topic. He adds that pretesting before teaching gives a baseline for measuring progress, which schools rarely do even for vocabulary. The move is to turn a cognitive-science finding into a blunt, implementable classroom rule.
points: Renaming retrieval practice as a test changes behaviour: every student answers, the timer runs and marking is taken seriously.
Salles claims retesting beats reteaching, so interventions after an assessment should require students to reproduce full-mark answers rather than be retaught content.
Sampling a whole topic with multiple-choice questions builds memory of the untested but related material better than examining one slice of it.
Multiple-choice pretests before teaching both direct attention to plausible alternatives and give the baseline schools need to measure progress.
quotes: There is hardly any retrieval. There is very little thinking hard. Not enough students buy into it and, though all teachers see the value of retrieval, very few make sure that all students retrieve.
Each student tries to answer more questions. Each student tries to get answers right. Each teacher makes sure that students take it seriously, because it is a test.
Implication – you must have regular low stakes testing to build memory.

Implication - testing is more effective than reteaching. Any interventions you do as a result of an assessment should not be re-teaching content, or skills, but retesting it. By all means model what success looks like, by showing students full mark answers, but require students to reproduce these, or similar answers, with more testing, not teaching.
Another huge advantage of this, of course, is that the pretest gives you a baseline. Now you can measure progress.

Do you test at the beginning of the year, to see what vocabulary each student knew already before you taught it? Probably not. Should you? Well, if you aren’t measuring progress, what are you measuring?
